text: A relation is a table made of rows (tuples) and columns (attributes). Each row represents one record, and each column holds values of one type.
A primary key is a minimal set of attributes that uniquely identifies each row in a table. A primary key cannot contain NULL values.
A foreign key is an attribute in one table that refers to the primary key of another table. Foreign keys enforce referential integrity between related tables.
A candidate key is any minimal set of attributes that could identify a row. A table can have several candidate keys but only one primary key. The candidate keys not chosen are called alternate keys.
The SELECT statement retrieves rows from a table. The WHERE clause filters individual rows before any grouping takes place.

GROUP BY groups rows that share values so that aggregate functions such as COUNT, SUM and AVG can be applied to each group. The HAVING clause filters groups after aggregation, whereas WHERE filters individual rows before aggregation.
ORDER BY sorts the result set. The default order is ascending (ASC), and DESC reverses it.
The DISTINCT keyword removes duplicate rows from the result set. COUNT(*) counts all rows, while COUNT(column) ignores NULL values in that column.
An INNER JOIN returns only the rows where the join condition matches in both tables. Rows with no match in the other table are left out.
A LEFT JOIN returns every row from the left table, together with the matching rows from the right table. Where there is no match, the columns from the right table are filled with NULL.
A FULL OUTER JOIN returns all rows from both tables, filling in NULL where either side has no match.
A CROSS JOIN returns the Cartesian product of two tables, pairing every row of the first table with every row of the second. If the tables have m and n rows, the result has m times n rows.
A self join joins a table to itself using table aliases to tell the two copies apart. It is used for hierarchical data, such as employees and their managers.
To find rows in the left table that have no match in the right table, use a LEFT JOIN and filter with WHERE on a right-table column IS NULL. This is known as the anti-join pattern.

A WHERE filter on a right-table column in a LEFT JOIN removes the rows where that column is NULL, so the query behaves like an INNER JOIN. To keep the outer join behaviour, put the condition in the ON clause instead.
First normal form (1NF) requires that every attribute holds a single atomic value. Repeating groups and multi-valued attributes, such as a column storing a comma-separated list, break 1NF.
A functional dependency X to Y means that each value of X determines exactly one value of Y. A dependency is partial when a non-key attribute depends on only part of a composite primary key.

Second normal form (2NF) removes partial dependencies, so every non-key attribute depends on the whole of the primary key. Partial dependencies are removed in 2NF, and the table must already be in 1NF. Third normal form (3NF) builds on this by removing transitive dependencies.
Third normal form (3NF) removes transitive dependencies, where a non-key attribute depends on another non-key attribute rather than directly on the key.

Boyce-Codd normal form (BCNF) is stricter than 3NF: for every functional dependency X to Y, X must be a superkey. A table in 3NF can still violate BCNF when a non-key attribute determines part of a candidate key.

A decomposition into smaller tables must be lossless, meaning that joining the new tables back together reproduces the original table with no spurious rows. A decomposition is lossless if the common attributes of the two new tables form a key of at least one of them.

An index is a separate data structure that lets the database find rows without scanning the whole table. Indexes speed up reads but slow down inserts, updates and deletes because the index must also be maintained.
Most relational databases use B-tree indexes by default. A B-tree index supports equality searches and range searches, such as BETWEEN, and keeps its keys in sorted order.
A clustered index determines the physical order of rows in the table, so a table can have only one clustered index.
A hash index supports only equality lookups. It cannot be used for range queries or for sorting.
A composite index on (a, b) can be used by queries that filter on a, or on a and b, but generally not by queries that filter only on b. This is known as the leftmost prefix rule.
Low-cardinality columns, such as a boolean flag, are usually poor candidates for a B-tree index because each value matches a large fraction of the table.
